text: This course opened with one question: how does SQL, the language you already know deeply through T-SQL, actually change across other platforms? Ten chapters and sixty-two lessons later, the answer has one clear shape, and it showed up over and over, in nearly every chapter. Querying fundamentals are remarkably portable. Procedural code is where the real divergence lives. That's the single throughline connecting everything you've just finished.

SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, and window functions behaved close to identically across every platform this course covered. Chapter 4's comparison of joins, CTEs, set operations, and window functions showed this directly, and the capstone, last lesson, proved it with a real query: the same join graph, the same GROUP BY, the same CTE, the same RANK OVER, worked structurally unchanged on T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL alike. The differences that remained were always small and specific -- a concatenation operator, a pagination keyword, a quoting convention -- never the underlying shape of the query itself.

Stored procedures, functions, triggers, and error handling told a completely different story. Chapters 5 through 8 spent dozens of lessons on exactly this: T-SQL's TRY CATCH has no literal equivalent on MySQL. Oracle's packages are a concept T-SQL simply doesn't have. Cursors behave differently enough on all four platforms that no automated tool can safely translate them. That's exactly why both migration lessons in this chapter independently landed on the same conclusion: migration tools handle querying syntax well and procedural code poorly, for a real structural reason -- not a tooling gap that's going to quietly get fixed in the next release.

So what does this mean for you, going forward? T-SQL fluency does not automatically transfer to a new platform's procedural idioms -- and that's fine, because this course never claimed it would. What it gave you instead is the ability to recognize the shape of the question the moment you hit a new platform: is this a querying difference, usually small, usually a fast lookup -- or a procedural difference, usually real, usually worth deliberately learning that platform's own idioms before you write production code against it.

The single most practical habit to carry forward: start, today, on whatever platform you touch next, a running personal cheat sheet. Not this course's cheat sheet -- yours. Every time a real difference costs you a lookup on a real job, write down the one line that would have saved you the trouble, and note which platform, which version. Lesson 59's own five-item pitfall checklist is exactly the kind of thing this habit produces, and that only took one course to build. A career's worth of platforms will build you a far longer, far more personally useful one.

You came into this course already fluent in T-SQL. You're leaving it able to recognize, on sight, which part of a new dialect will transfer easily and which part genuinely needs its own deliberate attention -- and with a real, worked example proving it, from the capstone, and a checklist for catching the pitfalls before they reach production. That's what staying fluent across platforms actually looks like. Congratulations on finishing SQL Dialects for Developers.
